controlLoop.label: Setpoint
controlLoop.description: The target the mechanism should reach
controlLoop.details: Every closed-loop movement starts with a setpoint — a target position, heading, or velocity. It might be a lift height in ticks, a drivetrain heading in degrees, or a flywheel RPM. The setpoint is the single source of truth the rest of the loop works to satisfy.

controlLoop.label: Feedback
controlLoop.details: A sensor reports the mechanism's real state every loop cycle — a motor encoder for position, an IMU for heading, an encoder delta for velocity. This feedback is what separates closed-loop control from open-loop timing: the robot reacts to reality instead of assuming a command worked.

controlLoop.label: Error
controlLoop.details: Error is the gap between where the mechanism should be and where it actually is. The controller's entire job is to drive this number to zero. A large error means push hard; a small error means ease off. Every term in the PID controller is computed from this single value and its history.

controlLoop.label: PID
controlLoop.details: The PID controller converts error into a correction. The proportional term responds to the current error, the integral term eliminates steady-state offset that P alone leaves behind, and the derivative term damps overshoot by reacting to how fast the error is changing. Balancing the three gains is what makes motion snappy but stable.

controlLoop.label: Feedforward
controlLoop.details: Feedforward adds the effort we know a mechanism will need before the error even appears — gravity compensation to hold a lift, static friction to break stiction, velocity terms to sustain motion. PID then only has to correct the small leftover error, which means lower gains, less overshoot, and far smoother movement.

controlLoop.label: Output
controlLoop.details: The combined PID + feedforward output is clamped to a safe range and written to the motor or servo. Then the loop immediately repeats — reading feedback, recomputing error, correcting again — dozens of times per second. That continuous cycle is what holds a position under load or drives to an exact point on the field.

techniques.title: Motion Profiling
techniques.description: Instead of commanding a mechanism straight to its target, we generate a smooth trapezoidal or S-curve velocity profile that ramps acceleration up and back down. This limits jerk, protects the hardware, and keeps the robot from tipping or slipping during aggressive moves.

techniques.title: Feedforward Models
techniques.description: For lifts and arms we model the physics — gravity, friction, and velocity — and feed that predicted effort in directly. PID is left to correct only the small residual error, which dramatically improves smoothness and lets us run lower, safer gains.

techniques.title: Live Gain Tuning
techniques.description: PID gains are exposed to FTC Dashboard so we can tune them live on the practice field without recompiling and redeploying. A tune that used to take an afternoon now takes a few minutes of watching the response curve settle.

techniques.title: Driver Assists
techniques.description: Teleop isn't purely manual. Heading-lock holds the robot square to the field, field-centric drive keeps controls intuitive regardless of orientation, and slow-mode scales inputs for fine alignment. The driver commands intent; the control code handles the precision.
